title: Footballs and doctored unisons
summary: Hinton's string overdubs and the out-of-tune unison.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: For example, I -- and I guess you do, too, being an acoustical bass player, all I ever see is one bass, two cellos, four horns and two violas on a date now. And I put on an earphone and I hear the rhythm section, and sometimes I hear the artist. Sometimes I never see the artist, I don't know who I'm recording with. But I will dub and do the sweetening with the string section. And I'm playing football, as we call whole notes the bass and the string section is playing these footballs behind them, big squeak.
Well, the arrangers don't know how to write for strings so they just write, whole note. That's why they call them footballs, they look like footballs.

And then they'll do that, and then they'll say, well, the bass is out now, and they'll give the five violins violas and two and the two cellos on one piece of music, which is And you've got seven making it play the second part./ And makes it sound like you've got 14 there.

Yeah. I've done dates like that where they'll hold you over and say, pull your slides out a little bit because it sounds like only one horn, so play a little out of tune on one track so it will sound like more than one horn. We had a unison once that was too good. He said, only one horn is playing there, there's four of you guys. We said, well, it's unison. But I only hear one horn. So I said, well, I'll tell you what, we'll tell one guy push in,
we'll pull out a little bit. It was really out of tune and rotten. He said, good, that's it. That's it. Now, it sounds like a unison.
